output.brief: The gap looks mostly like a difference in eligibility, not a bias against remote work. Only about a third of remote staff (32%) have the 18 months in their current level that the policy requires, against about 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are almost the same (20.0% remote vs 21.1% office). Matching the office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2% for remote staff, and the observed rate is 7.6%. That is a close fit. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a modest real difference can't be ruled out. The dashboard divides by all staff, so it mixes tenure with location. Requiring office days would not fix the main driver, would hit about 180 remote staff hired on home-based contracts, and has no support in this evidence. Don't confirm the proximity-bias diagnosis or announce the rule. Put it on hold. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check that at the FY2027 cycle. Separately, find out whether remote staff get fewer stretch assignments. The staffing data can't answer that, and the managers' comments hint at it. Also check why remote staff are newer, and whether more of them leave. I'm fairly confident in the main finding, less so on the smaller questions.
